title: Design Reviews
description: Lead and participate in architecture design reviews. Learn how to write Architecture Decision Records, evaluate trade-offs, give constructive feedback, and create documentation that outlasts the team.

data.text: Design reviews are where good architecture becomes great architecture. They are not gatekeeping — they are knowledge sharing. A well-run design review catches problems early, spreads institutional knowledge, and aligns the team on long-term direction.
As a senior engineer, you will both present your designs and review others. Both roles require preparation, humility, and clear communication.

An Architecture Decision Record (ADR) is a short document that captures an important architectural decision, its context, and its consequences. ADRs are the memory of your system. Six months from now, when someone asks 'why did we choose PostgreSQL over DynamoDB?', the ADR answers that question.

data.title: ADR Template
data.content: A typical ADR contains five sections:
data.code:
# ADR 012: Choose PostgreSQL for the orders database

## Status
Accepted

## Context
We need a transactional database for the orders service. The workload is write-heavy with complex joins for reporting.

## Decision
We will use PostgreSQL 15 with connection pooling via PgBouncer.

## Consequences

Positive:
- Strong ACID guarantees for financial transactions
- Mature ecosystem and tooling
- JSON support for flexible order attributes

Negative:
- Vertical scaling limits at very high write throughput
- Requires careful index management

## Alternatives Considered
- DynamoDB: rejected because complex reporting queries require joins
- MySQL: rejected because our team has deeper PostgreSQL expertise

data.text: Reviewers should evaluate designs across multiple dimensions. A design that is technically elegant but impossible to operate is not a good design. Use a checklist to make reviews consistent and thorough.

items.text: Does the design meet all functional and non-functional requirements?

items.hint: Look for an ADR or a trade-off analysis section

items.text: How does this design handle failure?
items.hint: Check for circuit breakers, retries, timeouts, and graceful degradation
Estimate cloud spend, monitoring overhead, and on-call burden

items.text: Can the team operate this at 3am?
items.hint: Consider debugging, rollback, and runbook complexity

items.text: Is the data model appropriate for the access patterns?
items.hint: Review queries, indexes, and caching strategy

items.text: Are security and compliance requirements addressed?
items.hint: Look for authentication, authorization, encryption, and audit logging

data.text: Every architectural decision involves trade-offs. A trade-off analysis makes these explicit so that reviewers and stakeholders understand what is being gained and what is being sacrificed.

data.title: Common Trade-off Dimensions
items: Latency vs. consistency: do you need immediate reads or guaranteed accuracy?
Cost vs. performance: can you afford the faster option?
Simplicity vs. flexibility: will the design need to change often?
Time to market vs. technical debt: is a quick solution acceptable as a starting point?
Consistency vs. availability: what happens during a network partition?

data.text: The best feedback is specific, actionable, and kind. Instead of 'this is wrong,' say 'have you considered the impact of a cold start on p99 latency?' Instead of 'this is over-engineered,' say 'what is the simplest design that meets the SLO?'

data.title: Review Etiquette
data.text: Ask questions before making statements. Questions invite collaboration; statements invite defensiveness. 'What happens when the cache is cold?' is more productive than 'Your caching strategy is wrong.'

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: ADRs capture the why behind architectural decisions for future team members
Use a checklist to make reviews consistent and thorough
Trade-offs are inevitable — make them explicit and documented
Feedback should be specific, actionable, and respectful
The best designs are understandable, operable, and aligned with business goals
data.takeaway: Design reviews are a team sport. Prepare thoroughly, listen actively, and leave ego at the door.

items.question: Who should attend a design review?
items.answer: The design author, at least one senior engineer from another team, a product manager or tech lead, and an on-call or SRE representative if the design affects production operations. Five to eight people is ideal.

items.question: How long should a design review last?
items.answer: 45 to 60 minutes. Distribute the design document 24 hours before the meeting so attendees can read it. Use the meeting for discussion, not presentation.

items.question: What if I disagree with the design?
items.answer: State your concern clearly, explain the risk, and suggest an alternative. If the author disagrees and the risk is acceptable, accept the decision. Disagree and commit. If the risk is high, escalate to the tech lead.

data.title: Review a Notification System Design
data.description: Read the attached design document for a notification system that sends email, SMS, and push notifications. Write an ADR summary, complete the review checklist, and write three pieces of constructive feedback focusing on reliability, cost, and operational simplicity.
